positions.commentary: Qualcomm's success relies on a series of improbable 'miracle' moments, making it a business of exceptions rather than a predictable investment pattern.

The speaker describes Broadcom's strategy as rolling up the semiconductor industry, squeezing companies for profitability, and acting like a private equity firm using significant debt for acquisitions.

thesis: This episode argues that Qualcomm's traditional handset business model is facing significant headwinds from competition and customer pushback, yet the company possesses a unique ability to capture value due to its technological pioneering status and patent portfolio. The primary investment case rests on the belief that Qualcomm's strategic shift into automotive, IoT, and 5G RF frontend represents a viable future growth opportunity, while the blocked Broadcom takeover is viewed as a major win for maintaining its independence.

claims.claim: The stock was flat and Wall Street hated it because manufacturing operations and JVs required too much capital and tied up profits.
claims.quote: Wall Street kind of hates it because the manufacturing operations and the JVs require so much capital, and they're tying up all the profits of the company.

claims.claim: The stock remained flat until January 1999 when the company began selling its infrastructure business.
claims.quote: The stock gets punished basically all the way up until January of 1999, and a few interesting things happen.

claims.claim: In March 1999, Qualcomm sold its infrastructure business and base stations to Ericsson to stop capital intensive manufacturing.
claims.quote: In March of '99, they sell their infrastructure business, the base stations, to Ericsson, which was normally one of their competitors.

claims.claim: Kyocera bought Qualcomm's mobile phone business in December 1999, leaving the company to sell chips and licenses.
claims.quote: December of 1999, Kyocera buys Qualcomm's mobile phone business. They now officially just sell chips that they call QTC, the Qualcomm CDMA Technologies Group.

claims.claim: Qualcomm's total revenue is close to $40 billion annually, with 85% coming from their semiconductor business.
claims.quote: today, Qualcomm's total revenue is close to $40 billion annually, I think, of which 85% is their semiconductor business.

claims.claim: Qualcomm's total revenue is $44 billion, of which $37 billion is from the semiconductor business.
claims.quote: Yup, $37 billion of their $44 billion of revenue is semiconductor business.

claims.claim: Qualcomm had 57% market share in the US in 2G and 100% market share in countries like South Korea.
claims.quote: Fifty-seven percent market share in the US in 2G, 100% market share in countries like South Korea.

claims.claim: Qualcomm did $383 million in revenue in 1995 and $814 million in revenue in 1996.
claims.quote: Qualcomm does $383 million in revenue in 1995. In 1996, they do $814 million in revenue.

claims.claim: 85% of today's Qualcomm revenue would not exist without the strategic decision to become a fabless semiconductor company.
claims.quote: But for this strategic decision, 85% of today's Qualcomm revenue would not exist.

claims.claim: Qualcomm is a technological pioneer with amazing value capture, holding a $120 billion market cap equivalent to the dot-com bubble peak and Broadcom's offer.
claims.quote: Qualcomm today has a $120 billion market cap. Which two things, (1) that's astonishing, that's impressive. They're technological pioneers and they're amazing at value capture. (2) That is the same prize that it was worth at the peak of the dot-com bubble.

claims.claim: Qualcomm is an amazingly high growth rate company with revenues growing 32% and earnings growing 47% year over year.
claims.quote: Revenues are growing 32%. Earnings are growing 47% year over year. This is an amazingly high growth rate company.

claims.claim: Qualcomm faces real competition from the low end from Mediatek, which surpassed Qualcomm in units shipped and uses cheaper chips.
claims.quote: Qualcomm has very real competition from the low end that we didn't talk about. An example is Mediatek who not only makes the baseband modem chip, but also systems on a chip using the stock ARM CPU designs. Mediatek systems are way cheaper than Qualcomm. I think they just surpassed Qualcomm in terms of the number of units shipped. All the low and mid-end Android phones are using Mediatek.

claims.claim: The speaker describes Broadcom's strategy as rolling up the semiconductor industry, squeezing companies for profitability, and acting like a private equity firm using significant debt for acquisitions.
claims.quote: The Broadcom strategy is to roll up the semiconductor industry, squeeze them as much as possible. In fact, they're basically a private equity firm. Broadcom is borrowing lots and lots of debt to make the acquisitions that they're making and then squeezing them for profitability.

claims.claim: The speaker views the blocked Broadcom takeover as a major win for Qualcomm due to its strong relationships with the US government and its ability to call in a favor regarding national security concerns.
claims.quote: This, I think, ends up being a big win for Qualcomm's lobbyists. I think they had great relationships with the US government and always have since the early days in being a government contractor. A lot of people that we talked to or at least that I talked to, viewed this as Qualcomm being able to call in a favor and say, this is a national security concern, don't you think?

claims.claim: The speaker considers the blocked Broadcom deal an enormous win for America and for Qualcomm, keeping it an independent American company despite the deal potentially going through.
claims.quote: This deal was going to go through, and Qualcomm was going to be everything you were just talking about with Broadcom, which would've been very—especially now, we know about semiconductors. This is one of the huge wins of the Trump administration for America was keeping Qualcomm an independent American company.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that while Qualcomm won the short term because Intel's modem failed, Apple likely won in the long term by buying the division away.
claims.quote: It's actually unclear who really wins here. I think Qualcomm wins in the short term because Apple's backup solution of Intel's modem fell entirely behind. But in the long term, what ended up happening is Apple actually bought that division away

claims.claim: The speaker describes Qualcomm as having gotten greedy by leveraging standard patents to charge excessive fees, leading to a lawsuit alleging abuse of the market.
claims.quote: The way that I essentially perceive this and why Apple eventually initiated the lawsuit is Qualcomm got greedy. They had patents on technologies that were part of standards that were set by industry consortiums all over the world, and they leveraged those patents in basically every way possible.

claims.claim: The speaker states that Apple paid $4 billion to secure patent licenses over the next 6 years after settling with Qualcomm in 2019.
claims.quote: Apple also paid $4 billion—now switching over the licensing side of the house—to secure the patent licenses over the next 6 years. I think $4.5 billion for a six-year deal.

claims.claim: Qualcomm faces strong competition from cheaper alternatives like Mediatek in the low-end market, and their aggressive licensing strategy has upset major customers like Samsung and Apple, potentially eroding their royalty leverage.
claims.quote: Qualcomm has very real competition from the low end that we didn't talk about. An example is Mediatek who not only makes the baseband modem chip, but also systems on a chip using the stock ARM CPU designs. Mediatek systems are way cheaper than Qualcomm. I think they just surpassed Qualcomm in terms of the number of units shipped. All the low and mid-end Android phones are using Mediatek.

claims.claim: Qualcomm's aggressive tactics have upset major customers like Samsung and Apple, leading them to develop their own silicon or consider alternatives, which threatens Qualcomm's ability to charge royalties.
claims.quote: The goal for Qualcomm should have been make as much money as you can without pissing people off too much. I think over the last decade, they really upset Samsung, Apple, so many people that are starting to at least make their own radios or even consider systems on a chip. Now that there's very viable alternatives for silicon that people can either use in-house or competitors coming around at diffe

claims.claim: The speakers believe the best days for Qualcomm's traditional handset business model are behind them as customers catch on to their strategies and squeeze them from multiple directions.
claims.quote: In order for the next decade as successful, they need to be absolutely correct about their growth businesses around IoT, around automotive, and around whatever the intelligent connected edge ends up describing. Because I think those are technologies that we don't quite know what they are yet. I think if they continue to try to run the same playbook in just the handset market that they have been, t

claims.claim: While the lawsuit situation could be a bear case, it might also be a bull case if Qualcomm continues to win in court and keep making tons of money.
claims.quote: The bull case, maybe the lawsuit thing is actually a bull case. They manage to keep making more and more money and have been reaffirmed over and over again in a bunch of jurisdictions that they set their way out of these lawsuits, but they're able to keep making tons of money.

claims.claim: The primary bull case for Qualcomm is the belief that their shift into automotive, IoT, and 5G RF frontend is a real and viable business opportunity.
claims.quote: The big bull case is you believe that this shift to automotive IoT and 5G RF frontend is real. For those keeping track at home, everything I'm about to say is a part of the chip segment that does that $37 billion in revenue. Automotive does $2 billion in revenue. That's a very real business. The RF frontend business that we were talking about, that does $4 billion a year in revenue.

claims.claim: The last decade was the best for Qualcomm's business model, and they were in the right place at the right time to capitalize on mobile.
claims.quote: My takeaway on Qualcomm is the last decade was basically the best decade for their business model and being in the right place at the right time to have an incredible business model around capitalizing on mobile.

claims.claim: Qualcomm's business exists because of the US regulatory system and patent rulings that allow them to capture significant value, representing a perfect execution of the game.
claims.quote: I do think the big picture is that the US government's patent system has granted Qualcomm a monopoly. This is one of the few things we've covered on the show where the business exists because of the US's regulatory system. They've basically said and then reaffirmed in a lot these rulings, you are allowed to capture a ton of value from this. There's so many good debates about whether the patent sys
